The Zuǒshì tradition considers Yù Quán's armed remonstrance to be an act of loving his lord,
and Wén Gōng's presenting of betrothal gifts to be an employment of ritual propriety.
The Gǔliáng tradition considers Wèi Zhé's refusal to admit his father to be an act of honoring his ancestor,
and not admitting Zǐ Jiū to be an act of internalizing evil.
The Gōngyáng tradition considers Jì Zhòng's deposing of his ruler to be an exercise of expediency,
and a concubine-mother being called "Lady" to be in accord with what is correct.
To consider armed remonstrance as loving one's lord
is to say that a ruler may be coerced.
To consider presenting betrothal gifts as an employment of ritual propriety
is to say that one may marry while in a period of mourning.
To consider refusing one's father as honoring one's ancestor
is to say that a son may be rebellious.
To consider not admitting Zǐ Jiū as internalizing evil
is to say that an enemy may be tolerated.
To consider deposing a ruler as an exercise of expediency
is to say that the divine vessel of the state may be coveted.

Preface to the Collected Explanations of the Gǔliáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals
In the past, the Way of the Zhōu dynasty declined and fell into ruin.
The bonds of Heaven were severed.
Rites were corrupted and music collapsed.
The constant principles of human relationships were destroyed.
Regicides, rebels, usurpers, and thieves were found in the states.
The dissolute who destroyed righteousness stood shoulder to shoulder.
For this reason, ominous portents and disasters arose in response to these transgressions.
The customs of the people were stained by this influence and changed.
Because of this, Yīn and Yáng exceeded their proper measures.
Because of this, the movements of the Seven Luminaries became irregular.
Because of this, rivers and great mountains collapsed and ran dry.
Because of this, the ghosts and spirits brought forth calamity and pestilence.
When affection between father and son was lacking,
then the critique in 'Xiǎo Biàn' arose.
When the rites between ruler and minister were abandoned,
then the admonition in 'Sāng Hù' emerged.
When the way between husband and wife was severed,
then the piece 'Gǔ Fēng' was composed.
When the bonds between kinsmen were broken,
then the resentment in 'Jiǎo Gōng' was made manifest.
When the path of the gentleman was blocked,
then the poem 'Bái Jū' was written.
Answer to Yīn Zhòngkān's Question about Reburial and Performing the *Yú* Sacrifice Again
Yīn Zhòngkān asked Fàn Níng, saying,
"Xún Nè's proposal regarding the Empress Dowager's reburial
was based on the statement that there should be no *yú* sacrifice.
The court adopted this.
The *Essential Records* of Hè says,
'After three months, it should then cease.' Why is this?"
Níng answered, saying,
"Hè has no such text.
Perhaps some busybody fabricated it?
I have not seen Mǎ [Róng], Zhèng [Xuán], Hè [Xún], or Fàn [Níng] say
that there is a *yú* sacrifice for a reburial.
The spirit is already in the ancestral temple;
what would be the purpose of the *yú* sacrifice?"
*Tōngdiǎn*, 120.
Answer to Wáng Huì's Question about Changing and Removing Mourning Garments
Wáng Huì asked Fàn Níng, saying,
"If a person, whose father is still alive, is mourning for their mother,
and only after seventeen months is the burial able to take place,
should they then immediately remove the mourning garments?
Or should they perform the *liàn* and *xiáng* sacrifices again?"
He answered, saying,
"For one whose burial takes place after the three-year [mourning period],
one must perform the later sacrifices—
that is, the *liàn* and *xiáng* sacrifices.
The chief mourner does not remove the garments;
before the burial, there is no change.
